scams.name: Airport & Peak Tram Taxi Overcharge
scams.description: A minority of red urban taxis at Hong Kong International Airport (HKIA) and the Peak Tram terminal refuse the meter and quote flat fares of HK$400–600 for rides the meter would put at HK$100–270. The benchmark case is Nick Toczek, a 72-year-old British children's-poetry writer, charged HK$600 for an HKIA to North Point ride in Feb 2023 (SCMP Mar 18, 2023); the Transport Department recorded a 69% spike in overcharging complaints that quarter. A Shenzhen Bay to HKIA visitor was charged HK$600 vs the normal HK$228–278 (SCMP Jun 8, 2024). SCMP's Aug 2014 Peak Tram investigation found drivers quoting HK$350–450 vs metered HK$50. Operation 'Firststrike' (Aug 2023) arrested two drivers and issued ten summonses after a HK$200-vs-HK$60 Lan Kwai Fong to Causeway Bay overcharge went viral. The Taxi Driver Demerit Point System launched Sep 22, 2024 with 10 points for overcharging (15-point two-year suspension ceiling); four drivers were sanctioned in the first month. April 2026 saw a 31-year-old driver arrested for an illegal HK$85 'highway toll' on a Disneyland–HKZMB run.
scams.avoidance: From HKIA take the Airport Express (HK$115 single, 24 min to Hong Kong Station) or open HKTaxi / Fly Taxi / Uber before leaving arrivals. At the Peak, walk to Exchange Square for the 15 bus (HK$11.20) rather than the Garden Road taxi stand. Photograph the red taxi's plate number before loading luggage; confirm the meter is running before the cab moves. Pay by Octopus or HKTaxi in-app where possible; always request the paper receipt (drivers are legally required to issue one on request). Inside city limits insist on the meter — meter-only is the law at Vienna-style Standplätze. File complaints with the Transport Department Passenger Liaison Group on 2889 9999 within 48 hours with plate number and pick-up stand. For fraud call 999 (emergency) or Police Report Room 2527 7177.
scams.location: HKIA arrivals taxi queue at Terminal 1; Peak Tram lower terminus taxi stand on Garden Road, Central; Shenzhen Bay and West Kowloon cross-boundary queues; evening ranks outside Lan Kwai Fong and Central

scams.name: Peninsula Centre Fake-Watch-Repair Shop
scams.description: A 'watch repair shop' at Peninsula Centre, Mody Road, Tsim Sha Tsui East took in two mainland customers' Patek Philippe and Rolex pieces worth HK$4.5 million on August 4, 2025, swapped them via a hidden door and a modified safe, and paid in counterfeit banknotes. Per The Standard (Feb 17, 2026), police arrested five suspects in rolling waves — the alleged mastermind and getaway driver on Aug 8, 2025; two local men aged 20 and 23 in late November; and a 58-year-old local on Feb 16, 2026, deported from Macau where he had allegedly run a near-identical scam via the HKZMB the same afternoon as the first heist. One watch and HK$60,000 cash recovered; the second million-dollar piece still missing. All five face conspiracy-to-defraud charges at West Kowloon Magistrates' Courts. A separate SCMP report (Aug 21, 2023) on a HK$3.5 million luxury-goods ring caught using fake cheques and forged bank slips shows the counterfeit-payment-for-real-goods pattern is established. For lower-stakes tourists, the same architecture shows up at the Sim City Computer Centre on Nathan Road and unmarked stalls on Sai Yeung Choi Street South in Mong Kok where r/HongKong's 'Camera buying advice - DX Zone SIM City' thread warns off the specific district.
scams.avoidance: Buy luxury watches only from manufacturer-authorized boutiques in IFC Mall, Pacific Place, Elements, or the Landmark — Patek Philippe, Rolex, Omega, and Audemars Piguet all have directly-operated Hong Kong stores with serial-traceable paperwork and dated warranty cards. For electronics use Apple ifc mall, Fortress (Wharf T&T's chain), or Broadway — not Sim City or unmarked Mong Kok stalls. Before handing over any luxury item for 'cleaning' or 'service,' get a written receipt with the shop's full Business Registration (BR) number and photograph the shopfront and interior. Learn the three big HK$1,000 security features — bauhinia-flower watermark, raised printing, colour-shift '1000' — and check every large note. Report counterfeit cases to Customs 24-hour hotline 182 8080 and ADCC Anti-Scam Helpline 18222; Consumer Council handles bait-and-switch complaints at +852 2929 2222.
scams.location: Peninsula Centre, Mody Road, Tsim Sha Tsui East, Kowloon; knock-off versions near the Peninsula Hotel on Salisbury Road and in Causeway Bay watch arcades; adjacent pattern at Sim City Computer Centre and Sai Yeung Choi Street South in Mong Kok

scams.name: Tsim Sha Tsui & Causeway Bay Fake Monks
scams.description: Men in saffron robes with brass bowls slip a 'blessing' bracelet or amulet onto your wrist on Nathan Road, Russell Street, or at an MTR exit, then block your path and pressure you for HK$2,000 or a WeChat Pay transfer. SCMP first documented the pattern on March 8, 2008 ('Fake monks scam alms from unwary expats'), citing the Hong Kong Buddhist Association executive officer: 'people should not donate money to people just because they are dressed like monks and nuns.' A long-running Tripadvisor Hong Kong forum thread locates the scammers at Tsim Sha Tsui, Wan Chai, Central, and Ten Thousand Buddhas Monastery in Sha Tin, and reports that the men 'are from the Mainland China and speak Putonghua/Mandarin.' A Lemon8 2024 firsthand post gives the Wan Chai MTR variant: a bracelet was slipped onto the writer's wrist, a donation form already showing '2,000' was produced, and when she refused cash a WeChat Pay QR code appeared. Target set is selected by appearance: tourists, expatriates, and mainland visitors are approached; local Cantonese-speakers are skipped.
scams.avoidance: Keep hands in pockets or bag straps when approached and repeat 'no' while walking — do not stop. If an item is forced on you, drop it and continue walking — Hong Kong law does not bind you to a gift you did not accept. Never scan a street QR code; legitimate temples do not take alms this way. To donate to Buddhist causes properly, use hkbuddhist.org (Hong Kong Buddhist Association online donations to registered temples). If a 'monk' physically blocks you, call 999. For amounts already transferred, call ADCC Anti-Scam Helpline 18222 immediately and your bank's fraud line; the Scameter search engine at scameter.cyberdefender.hk lets you check a WeChat Pay ID, bank account, or phone number against the Hong Kong Police scam database.
scams.location: Avenue of Stars and Nathan Road/Salisbury Road junction in Tsim Sha Tsui; Times Square and Russell Street in Causeway Bay; Wan Chai MTR exits; Kansu Street end of Temple Street Night Market; Ten Thousand Buddhas Monastery in Sha Tin

scams.name: Mong Kok & Ladies' Market Counterfeit Run
scams.description: Hong Kong Customs ran 11 separate crackdowns in late 2025 on Tung Choi Street (Ladies' Market) and estimates the counterfeit tourist-market industry at tens of millions of HKD. On December 4–5, 2025, officers swept 21 fixed stalls on Tung Choi Street plus an upstairs warehouse, seized HK$2.58 million in handbags, leather goods, and jewellery, and arrested five people aged 23–56 (The Standard, Dec 5, 2025). Between December 8 and 19, 2025, Customs' Operation 'Santa Guardian' logged 28 cases and HK$36 million in seized counterfeits — about HK$33 million from logistics warehouses and HK$3.1 million at the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge inbound examination building (info.gov.hk Dec 29, 2025). The World Trademark Review reported Customs' 2023 total at 400 cross-boundary cases and over 620,000 counterfeit items worth HK$267 million. The most common mechanic on Tung Choi Street is straight fakes sold openly; the catch for first-timers is a back-room 'real' handbag swapped for a lesser copy during the thirty seconds you are writing down your email for the fake 'warranty.' Under the Trade Descriptions Ordinance (Cap. 362), possession of counterfeit goods for commercial purposes carries up to HK$500,000 fine and five years' imprisonment for sellers; buyers face no criminal penalty but fakes may be seized at UK, EU, or Australian customs on return.
scams.avoidance: For real designer goods use Lane Crawford, Harvey Nichols, or brand boutiques in IFC / Pacific Place / Elements. Look for the Q-Mark HKTB Quality Tourism Services decal (hktb.com/qts) on shop doors. Never hand over a deposit against tomorrow's collection at a street market — 'raid in progress' is a rush-close tactic. Keep the item in your sight through packing and pay only on final handover. For retail disputes call Consumer Council +852 2929 2222 (consumer.org.hk/complaint); for counterfeit-goods cases call the Customs 24-hour hotline 182 8080. Hong Kong Tourism Board visitor hotline +852 2508 1234 can direct you to the right desk. For anything that felt like fraud, not just overpricing: ADCC 18222 and Police Report Room 2527 7177.
scams.location: Tung Choi Street (Ladies' Market), Fa Yuen Street, Sai Yeung Choi Street South in Mong Kok; Temple Street Night Market; Stanley Market; Fortune Street in Cheung Sha Wan

scams.name: Mong Kok 'Massage' Wallet Theft
scams.description: A stranger on Tung Choi Street offers an HK$300 'massage' at a nearby guest house, walks you up, and empties your wallet while you are in the bathroom. The SCMP case file (Apr 25, 2019) is the cleanest statement of the pattern: a 28-year-old mainland Chinese woman was arrested at Tai On House on Tung Choi Street in Mong Kok — about 200 metres from Mong Kok Police Station — after approaching male tourists on the street, offering massage services, and walking them to guest houses. 'In both incidents,' police told SCMP, 'valuables and cash were stolen when the victims went to the toilet.' The two documented thefts included one HK$80,000 watch; police linked her to an earlier theft where a 58-year-old man lost HK$27,000 in a near-identical setup. Dotdotnews (Jun 23, 2024) on Sham Shui Po reported an ongoing surge in unlicensed massage storefronts priced 'from a few dozen to several hundred Hong Kong dollars' with 'additional charges' tacked on. An Expat Hong Kong Facebook post identified a persistent Wan Chai MTR variant: a man posing as stranded near the immigration footbridge asking lone women for taxi money. Hong Kong law allows purchase of services at unlicensed parlours but not their operation, which dampens the police-station incentive to file.
scams.avoidance: Book massage at licensed chain shops (Happy Foot, Ten Feet Tall, Rejuvenation) with posted price lists — HK$300–600/hour is normal. Refuse any street solicitation in Mong Kok, Sham Shui Po, or Wan Chai for massage, 'VIP service,' or spa treatments. Keep your wallet, phone, and passport in a zipped crossbody bag on your person at all times in a massage setting. If led upstairs from a street approach, turn around and leave — there is always a legitimate alternative on a street-level shopfront. For lone women approached at MTR exits with a taxi-fare story, walk away and report to the nearest MTR station staff or call 999. Report immediately to Mong Kok Police Station (22 Prince Edward Road West, +852 2381 2081) or Wan Chai Police Station (1 Arsenal Street, +852 2577 0911) if robbed. HKTB visitor hotline +852 2508 1234 for translation; ADCC 18222 for immediate fraud consultation.
scams.location: Tung Choi Street and Nathan Road side-alleys in Mong Kok; guest houses above shops near Tai On House; Sham Shui Po illicit massage storefronts on Cheung Sha Wan Road; Wan Chai MTR footbridge at night

scams.name: MTR Pickpocket Ring
scams.description: Operation 'Darkvale' in September 2023 arrested a six-person mainland pickpocket syndicate linked to 19 MTR cases, and Hong Kong Police warned citywide pickpocket reports were up 212% year-on-year. SCMP's September 19, 2023 report put the shape of the problem on record: eleven mainland Chinese travellers were arrested among a total of 50 in the operation; six of those eleven were alleged syndicate members holding two-way permits for Hong Kong entry, linked to 19 documented MTR cases and 106 overall theft reports. Inspector Lam Kin-yu of the Railway District explained: 'They usually work in a group of two or three people and commit the crimes in crowded areas. They then bring the stolen goods back to the mainland for distribution.' Victims skewed toward women and the elderly. Lam's statistics: 228 pickpocket cases in Jan–Jun 2023 vs 73 in 2022 — a surge tied to post-COVID cross-boundary travel resumption. The mechanic is three people, one umbrella, and four seconds: one thief presses against you, one stands behind, one holds an umbrella or newspaper to block CCTV and the other passengers' line of sight, executed as the train decelerates or the door chime sounds. SCMP also documented a shopping-centre-toilet version using 'a hooked apparatus in cubicles' to lift bags from hangers in Harbour City, Times Square, and Festival Walk washrooms.
scams.avoidance: Wear bags crossbody with the zip against your chest; keep phone in a zipped front pocket, never a back pocket or a backpack mesh pouch. Turn your backpack to your front at Central / Admiralty escalators and on Tsuen Wan Line peak-hour trains — locals do it, you will not look out of place. Never hang your bag on a cubicle hook in a shopping-centre washroom — keep it on your lap. Carry only one card and HK$500–1,000 in small notes; leave the rest in the hotel safe. If lifted, call 999 first, then +852 2861 0020 for MTR Corporation Lost Property Office, then 2527 7177 for the Police Report Room. Use scameter.cyberdefender.hk to verify suspicious bank accounts the thieves may have used if cards were taken.
scams.location: Tsuen Wan Line through Tsim Sha Tsui, Mong Kok, Prince Edward and Sham Shui Po; Island Line between Central, Admiralty, and Causeway Bay; Airport Express platforms; Harbour City and Times Square shopping-centre toilets; escalators rising out of Central Station

scams.name: Peak Tram Phishing Website
scams.description: The Peak Tram Company issued an official warning on December 16, 2024 that counterfeit ticketing websites mimicking thepeak.com.hk are selling fake 'fast-track' tickets that either never arrive or resolve into a third-party tour desk at the terminus. Their official notice states: 'We have discovered counterfeit websites mimicking our official website and trying to sell fake tickets. Please exercise caution and don't engage with these sites.' The only official ticketing URL is ticketing.thepeak.com.hk; the company's PDF and Instagram post both ask visitors to call the ADCC Anti-Scam Helpline on 18222 if they suspect they have hit a phishing site. A Tripadvisor reviewer on the 'Peak Tram Fast-Track Guided Tour' listing described the third-party angle: 'Every time, the site shows tickets available, takes my money, then emails me saying the tickets aren't available. They hold your money for over a month.' The Peak Tram route — Garden Road, Central to The Peak, 1.3 km, HK$108 return adult — is the single most concentrated tourist bottleneck in Hong Kong. The mechanic has two flavours: a phishing website served via Instagram / Facebook ads with lookalike domains (peaktramhk.com, hkpeaktram.com, hongkongpeak-tram.com) that skims card details; and a tout in a branded-looking uniform in the Garden Road queue offering a 'fast track guided tour' for HK$300–400 that Peak Tram staff do not recognize.
scams.avoidance: Buy Peak Tram tickets only at ticketing.thepeak.com.hk or the 33 Garden Road terminus counter. For bundled tours, use only HKTB Q-Mark Quality Tourism Services-registered operators (hktb.com/qts). Check any website against scameter.cyberdefender.hk before entering card details. Decline all touts in the Garden Road queue and at Central Pier 7. For phishing losses, call your bank's 24-hour fraud line (major HK banks have dedicated dispute desks), ADCC Anti-Scam Helpline 18222, and file a report at police.gov.hk. HKTB visitor hotline +852 2508 1234 can direct non-resident victims to the right desk.
scams.location: Search results and Instagram/Facebook ads for 'Peak Tram tickets'; third-party reseller touts along Garden Road at the Peak Tram lower terminus and the queue for the Central Pier 7 Star Ferry

scams.name: Tsim Sha Tsui Tailor Deposit Disappearance
scams.description: A Tsim Sha Tsui 'bespoke tailor' offers a rush 24-hour suit for a 50% deposit (typically HK$1,500–3,000), and either the shutter is down the next day, the finish is unwearable, or the tailor demands 'extra fabric' charges to release the piece. Consumer Council Hong Kong (consumer.org.hk) publishes a monthly 'Class Action' list of poor traders that has repeatedly featured rush-tailor operators, and Reddit's r/HongKong 'What's a scam or not a good deal in Hong Kong that you'd warn tourists about' thread repeatedly flags Tsim Sha Tsui tailors as the single highest-volume tourist-trap complaint after electronics. The hierarchy: legitimate custom tailors such as Sam's Tailor (13 Burlington Arcade, 92–94 Nathan Road, est. 1957) work on five-to-seven-day fittings with multiple client visits and do not pressure cash deposits above 30% up front; the rush-tailor variant lives off deposits from people who have a cruise-ship or flight deadline. The mechanic is classic pre-payment fraud — a tout on Nathan Road walks you upstairs to a small shop, the fabric book is genuine, the fitting is quick, the price is 60% below your home market, and a 50% cash or WeChat-Pay deposit is demanded. Three outcomes: a wrong fitting with a firm balance demand before alterations; an additional HK$500–1,000 'imported fabric' charge; or a shuttered shop whose business name does not exist in Hong Kong's Companies Registry. These are contract-dispute tourist traps, not criminal fraud in the Peninsula Centre sense.
scams.avoidance: Choose established Hong Kong tailors: Sam's Tailor (Burlington Arcade, 92–94 Nathan Road, +852 2367 9423, est. 1957), Raja Fashions (Granville Road), WW Chan (Pacific Place), Empire Tailors (Hankow Road). Never pay more than 30% up front; always pay by credit card for chargeback protection (not WeChat / Alipay / cash). Read reviews that specifically mention receiving and wearing the finished suit, not just the fitting. Get the expected-ready date and Business Registration number in writing on the receipt. For disputes, contact Consumer Council +852 2929 2222 or consumer.org.hk/complaint within 30 days; for clear fraud where no shop exists call 999 and Police Report Room 2527 7177. The Hong Kong Tourism Board visitor hotline +852 2508 1234 has a Tourism Quality Service complaint referral desk for Q-Mark registered shops.
scams.location: Tailor shops around Nathan Road, Peking Road, Mody Road, and Kimberley Road in Tsim Sha Tsui; Hart Avenue and the Chungking Mansions / Mirador Mansion blocks; satellite cluster around Central's Lan Kwai Fong alleys
